title: Scalable Photon-Mediated Two-Qubit Gates with Spectrally Noisy Quantum Emitters
authors: Shreekanth S. Yuvarajan, W. A. Coish, David Hucul, Herbert F. Fotso
abstract: When two quantum bits are coupled through a cavity, a two-qubit gate can be realized between them either in the near-resonant regime over a timescale established by the coupling strength of the qubits with the cavity, or in the dispersive regime, over a longer timescale established by the combination of the coupling strength and the frequency detuning between the qubits and the cavity. When the qubits are spectrally noisy or differently detuned from the cavity, the fidelity for the operation can be drastically reduced in either case, precluding scalable realizations. We introduce the protocol for optimal cavity-enabled gates (POCEG) that is shown, through reliable numerical and analytical solutions, to overcome spectral differences between quantum bits and to achieve high fidelity between disparate/noisy quantum emitters. Namely, for a cavity with low damping rate, we apply a sequence of pulses to the qubits at the frequency of the cavity while periodically modulating the coupling of the qubits to the cavity. Alternatively, in the case of a large damping rate, we operate in the dispersive regime and overcome spectral disparities by applying the pulses at a frequency far-detuned from the cavity. In both instances, we find for the quantum state transfer between the two qubits that, with a modest inter-pulse delay, the fidelity that would otherwise be strongly suppressed by the spectral mismatch of the qubits can be increased beyond 99.9%. These protocols have the capacity to bring two-qubit gates between solid state systems across the threshold required for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
summary: The paper introduces the Protocol for Optimal Cavity-Enabled Gates (POCEG) to realize high-fidelity two-qubit gates between noisy qubits coupled via an optical cavity. By applying tailored pulsed sequences, the protocol successfully mitigates fidelity loss caused by spectral detuning in both low and high damping environments. This demonstrates a pathway toward scalable quantum computation using solid-state emitters.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is achieving high-fidelity two-qubit gates mediated by a cavity when the constituent qubits suffer from spectral noise or significant detuning.
main_result: A protocol (POCEG) was developed that successfully overcomes spectral mismatches, enabling state transfer fidelities exceeding 99.9% in both low and high damping rate regimes.
method: The authors employ theoretical analysis using the average Hamiltonian theory and time-dependent pulse sequences to engineer robust quantum gates.
model_or_system: The system consists of two solid-state qubits coupled to a single optical cavity mode. The dynamics are governed by a complex Hamiltonian incorporating time-dependent couplings and detunings, analyzed via master equations.
key_observables: State transfer fidelity ($F$), which is the primary metric; also analyzed are cavity occupation probabilities ($n_c$).
important_parameters: Qubit/Cavity detunings ($\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}$), cavity damping rate ($\kappa$), and control parameters like pulse sequence length or number of pulses ($N_p$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on perturbative expansions (e.g., Magnus expansion) assuming small inter-pulse delays ($	au$) relative to other timescales, and truncating the Hilbert space based on cavity excitation levels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate fidelity deterioration under uncontrolled evolution versus improvement using POCEG; they also map out the parameter space where high fidelity is maintained as a function of detuning and pulse number.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, develops the POCEG protocol for both low and high damping regimes (using different control sequences), derives an effective Hamiltonian via average Hamiltonian theory, and finally simulates state transfer fidelity to demonstrate robustness against spectral noise.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major bottleneck in solid-state quantum computing—decoherence due to spectral mismatch—by proposing engineered pulse sequences that stabilize gate operations. It bridges theoretical control techniques with practical platform limitations.
